masthead_title: Canada retaliates on tariffs; the tape shrugs
regime_line: Canada slapped retaliatory tariffs of 15–50% on about $20 billion of U.S. goods overnight, and the market treated it as background noise — long rates eased, credit stayed calm, and the average stock pushed to one of its strongest levels of the past six months, all ahead of tonight's high-stakes Nvidia earnings.

claims_section_html:
Claims ledger — nothing due today, one new claim opens

No claim hits its deadline this morning, so nothing gets graded — but one open claim gets a data point, and tonight's Nvidia print is important enough to log a new one.

  • CL-0004 — still open, due Friday (08-28). The question: does Walmart's soft sales-growth print mean the broader consumer is cooling, tested against whether consumer-discretionary stocks (XLY) lag the market by 1.5 points or more. No XLY reading qualified in today's mechanical scan, so there's no new number for the test itself — but a related data point leans supportive: the Conference Board's Consumer Confidence index fell to 89.4 in August, a seven-month low, missing the 90.3 consensus in our calendar, with the forward-looking expectations gauge dropping to 68.2, a level the Conference Board itself associates with recession risk within a year (Reuters via Investing.com). Suggestive, not dispositive — the actual test is still XLY vs. the market, graded Friday.
  • CL-0005 (new, due 2026-09-02) — Semiconductor stocks rallied broadly this morning (AMD +4.9%, Marvell +4.8%, Cadence +5.1%, Lumentum +6.7%, Coherent +4.6%) ahead of tonight's Nvidia earnings after the close — the biggest single event on the AI-capex watch this quarter. The question: is this durable conviction in AI-capex demand, or positioning that unwinds once the print lands? The test: SMH's cumulative return versus SPY, measured from today's close (08-25) through 2026-09-02, stays no worse than 2 percentage points of underperformance. A bigger shortfall than that would say today's rally got ahead of itself.
story_html:
This morning's headline is trade policy, not markets. Canada announced retaliatory tariffs of 15%, 25% and 50% on roughly $20 billion of U.S. goods — steel, dairy, appliances, farm equipment, and a long list of everyday items down to cheese and toilet paper — effective September 8, after the U.S. imposed 50% tariffs on Canadian goods over the weekend and trade talks broke down (CNBC, NPR, Washington Post). It's the sharpest escalation yet in a trade dispute that's been simmering for a year. And yet U.S. stocks rose right through it: the S&P 500 gained 0.3% to 7,677 and the Nasdaq climbed 0.7%, with reporting attributing the calm to investors looking past the tariff headlines toward two bigger catalysts this week — Nvidia's earnings after tonight's close and Fed Chair Kevin Warsh's first Jackson Hole speech Friday (Yahoo Finance).

Does the state file back up "markets are looking past this"? So far, yes, on every channel that would show stress first. Long rates eased rather than jumped (10-year −6bp to 4.64%, 30-year −6bp to 5.17%) — a tariff shock that truly worried the market about growth or inflation would more typically push yields up, not pull them down. Junk-bond spreads — HY OAS, the extra yield investors demand to lend to junk-rated companies, and the fastest tell for credit-market nerves — barely moved. And breadth, meaning the average stock rather than just the handful of giants, is unusually strong versus its own recent history (today's chart). Where this brief stays disciplined, per its political-neutrality rule: tariffs are treated here strictly as a mechanical margin and pass-through question for the named sectors, never as a verdict on the policy itself. If credit or breadth roll over as the September 8 tariff date approaches, this brief will say so — today, they haven't.
dashboard_lag_note: Observation dates in parentheses where they trail the 2026-08-25 market close: the TIPS real yield, breakeven, and both credit-spread series publish a day behind (§5), as does SOFR; Fed balance sheet and TGA are weekly (08-19). Flagged rows (⚑): far outside the past-6-months normal range — see the Reading key below.
dashboard_interp_html: The whole Tier 1 spine eased today, in the same direction as the equity move, which is why nothing here fights the "markets are calm" story above. The 10-year Treasury yield fell 6 basis points to 4.64% and the 30-year fell 6bp to 5.17%; both are still flagged (higher than on all but a handful of days in the past six months — z +1.12 and +1.24), so "still elevated but easing" is the more precise read than either "high" or "falling." The 2-year note, which moves mainly on where investors think the Fed is headed rather than on supply or term-premium, eased 7bp to 4.17% — a small dovish lean, not a repricing. Credit and plumbing stayed unremarkable: junk-bond spreads (still using Monday's 08-24 print) sit at 2.69%, comfortably inside their normal range and a touch below their own six-month average; the dollar (DXY) slipped modestly to 98.92. None of this is what a market bracing for a real trade-war growth shock would look like — it's a quiet plumbing morning underneath a loud policy headline.
movers_html:
How this section works: all 503 S&P constituents scanned mechanically; a stock qualifies only by moving >4% (>2.5% for the 50 biggest) — never by seeming interesting. 22 names and 1 sector divergence qualified today; cap is 3 names + a sector note. "Stated reason" is what reporting said, not necessarily what's true.

AMD +4.91% (479.18, from 456.75) — what happened: Advanced Micro Devices led a broad chip-sector rally. Stated reason: Raymond James upgraded the stock to Strong Buy and lifted its price target to $641 from $565, forecasting the server-CPU market will grow 44% a year to $201 billion by 2030 (TradingKey, 24/7 Wall St.). Why it matters: this is a direct AI-capex-demand read, and it's landing the night before Nvidia reports — the real test of whether today's optimism is durable (logged as CL-0005 below).

HOOD +8.17% (112.09, from 103.62) — what happened: Robinhood was today's second-biggest S&P mover. Stated reason: Goldman Sachs and Needham both raised price targets (Goldman to $123, Needham to $123) citing rising retail and crypto trading volumes and growing Wall Street interest in prediction markets — Bernstein projects roughly $240 billion in industry prediction-market volume for 2026 (GuruFocus, FX Leaders, CryptoTimes). Why it matters: a read on retail risk appetite and trading activity — consistent with, and a contributor to, today's broad-based breadth flag, not a separate story.

MRNA +14.36% (158.83, from 138.89) — what happened: Moderna was today's single biggest S&P mover, extending a volatile stretch. Stated reason: shares are rebounding after cooling off from the historic rally two weeks ago on positive Phase 3 results for its melanoma cancer vaccine, as investors reassess the commercial opportunity (Forbes, Yahoo Finance). Why it matters: idiosyncratic — no macro read-through. This is a single-company clinical-trial story, not a signal about the broader market or economy.

Sector note: Energy was today's worst-performing sector, 1.98 points behind the market (XLE −1.66% vs. SPY +0.32%). Stated reason: WTI crude fell about 3.1% to roughly $82/barrel, its second decline after a run of gains, as oil eased broader market anxiety (Washington Times, Forbes Advisor). Read-through: falling energy costs ease inflation and margin pressure economy-wide — consistent with today's cooler long rates and calm breakevens, and one more reason nothing here is confirming stress from the tariff headlines.
chart_of_day_why: The equal-weight S&P 500 (RSP) carries today's single largest watch-list flag (z +1.67, just ahead of copper's +1.63) — for the second day running, but for a different reason. Yesterday it meant "the damage is contained to one sector." Today, with the cap-weighted index also up and no sector under stress, it means something more constructive: strength is broad-based, not a few mega-caps carrying the tape — exactly the kind of breadth that should worry a market bracing for a trade-war-driven slowdown, and isn't here.
tier3_html:
Daily read: SMH (the semiconductor ETF — the AI-capex sector's most direct market proxy) rose 1.65% today as chip stocks bounced broadly: AMD (+4.9%), Marvell (+4.8%), Cadence Design Systems (+5.1%), Lumentum (+6.7%) and Coherent (+4.6%) all rallied together, several on analyst-upgrade news, heading into tonight's Nvidia earnings after the close — the single biggest event on this watch this quarter. SMH's own move isn't statistically unusual yet (z +0.32, inside normal range) and remains up 54.3% year-to-date; today reads as positioning into the print, not a signal on its own.

Financing watch: nothing new surfaced overnight on AI-adjacent debt issuance or vendor-financing structures specifically — the standing backdrop (roughly $225 billion in hyperscaler-and-related bond issuance so far this year, per S&P Global reporting) is unchanged rather than newly newsworthy today. Tonight's Nvidia print is the more immediate test of that financing story's durability; CL-0005 (above) sets out what would count as confirmation versus a false signal.
calendar_note_html: Today is an event day, framed rather than predicted (per this brief's own event-day rule): the Core PCE Price Index (8:30am ET, forecast 0.2% m/m vs. 0.1% prior) is the Fed's preferred inflation gauge, and a hot print would revive the inflation-fear reading of long rates that CL-0003 already tested and closed out this month — a soft or in-line print keeps that question closed. The Preliminary GDP reading (8:30am, forecast 1.5% q/q, matching last) is the growth-side counterpart. Both feed directly into Friday's bigger event: Fed Chair Kevin Warsh's first Jackson Hole speech as chair, where investors want a read on how he weighs inflation against growth heading into the September 16–17 FOMC meeting. Separately — and not on this macro calendar — Nvidia reports after tonight's close; see Tier 3 above.
concept_unit: Unit 1 · Yield curve mechanics · segment 6 of ~10
concept_title: Convexity — why duration is a good estimate, not an exact one
concept_html: Yesterday's concept was duration — the ruler that predicts how much a bond's price moves for a given change in yield. Today's twist: that ruler bends. Duration is really just the slope of the price-versus-yield relationship at today's yield — a straight-line approximation of something that's actually curved. As yields fall, bond prices rise a little faster than duration alone predicts; as yields rise, prices fall a little slower than duration predicts. That curvature is convexity, and it's a genuine advantage to the bondholder — gains get a boost, losses get a cushion — which is also part of why highly convex bonds trade at a premium (a lower yield) to begin with. It barely shows up on a quiet day like today, when the 10-year and 30-year both eased a modest 6 basis points; duration alone explains almost all of a move that small. It matters most on the big moves — the kind this month's 30-year selloff produced, and the kind tonight's Nvidia print or Friday's Jackson Hole speech could still produce — where the straight-line estimate starts drifting from what the tape actually does.
client_translation: "Your bond fund doesn't gain or lose in a perfectly straight line as rates move — it's built with a little extra cushion on the downside and a little extra kick on the upside, which is one more reason a long-term bond fund isn't quite as scary as a simple 'how much will rates hurt me' number makes it sound."

Markets didn't price it as a growth shock — rates eased, credit stayed calm — but it's a real margin and pass-through question for the named sectors worth watching as the effective date nears.

Early, supportive-leaning evidence for the open Walmart-consumer question (CL-0004, graded Friday) — not yet conclusive.
